paper_title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher's log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain--student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Reinforcement learning can improve language-model instruction following using rewards learned from human preferences (Ouyang et al., 2022), and mathematical and code reasoning using verifiable Corresponding author.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: rewards (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). The latter requires repeated generation, verification, and optimization of on-policy responses. Reusing teachers RL improvements offers way to share this training effort across target models. This raises the question: which local changes in the teachers policy should guide student on its own generated trajectories? Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student to match the teachers token distributions on student-generated prefixes (Agarwal et al., 2024). Its supervision remains tied to the teachers absolute policy and capability limitations. On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD2) uses the change between reasoning-tuned teacher and its base model, retaining token-level signals when the centered change agrees in sign with the centered standard distillation signal (Heo et al., 2026). Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) focuses on RL-induced improvements. It uses the log-probability ratio between pre-RL and post-RL teacher checkpoints as dense implicit reward on student-generated states, transferring the teachers policy change without matching its absolute distribution (Feng et al., 2026). Both methods extract changes from pair of teacher models, but neither directly measures whether consecutive changes during teacher RL point in compatible directions. The Initial-to-Final log-probability ratio captures only the change between the teachers policies before and after RL training. The same endpoint signal can arise from early and late policy changes that point in similar or opposing directions. Endpoint-only transfer cannot distinguish these cases. We hypothesize that agreement between the early and late changes provides evidence for deciding how much weight to assign an endpoint shift at student-generated prefix. Building on this hypothesis, we propose Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to gate the endpoint transfer signal. We retain three checkpoints from the same teacher RL run: Initial before RL, Waypoint at an intermediate RL step, and Final at the end of RL. At each student-generated prefix, we select its top-k most probable next-token candidates. Over these candidates, we compare how the teachers relative preferences change from Initial to Waypoint and from Waypoint to Final. Their agreement gates the centered Initial-to-Final signal, retaining aligned changes and suppressing reversals. Waypoint thus supplies evidence for weighting the endpoint shift, which remains the transferred signal. Relative to endpoint-only transfer, this requires one additional frozen teacher scoring pass, with no new teacher training or verifier calls during student transfer. Our contributions are: Temporal agreement as criterion for selective transfer. We use the Waypoint checkpoint to assess temporal agreement at student-generated prefixes, revealing directional information unavailable from the endpoint pair alone. Waypoint-guided gating of endpoint signals. We develop Waypoint-OPD, dense onpolicy objective that uses this agreement to weight the endpoint signal at each studentgenerated prefix, with one additional frozen teacher scoring pass. Higher average performance across domains and model sizes. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B(Yang et al., 2025) on mathematics and code. WaypointOPD achieves the highest recorded domain average among the evaluated baselines in all six settings (Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2). Ablations on Qwen3-8B mathematical reasoning support the value of temporal gating  (Table 3)  .

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We examine three questions: Q1. Does Waypoint-OPD improve transfer across math, code, and model scales? Q2. Does temporal consistency improve on endpoint transfer and Final-teacher imitation? Q3. How do gate assignment, mean normalization, and Waypoint position affect performance? Supplementary training-time and response-length analyses appear in Appendix H. 4.1 MODELS, DATA, AND EVALUATION Teacher checkpoints and student models. For each domain, we use three checkpoints from the same Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) RL run: Initial (π0) before RL, Waypoint (πm) at RL step 600, and Final (π1) at RL step 1200. Math and code teachers use non-thinking RL. All three checkpoints remain frozen during transfer. We train Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B students using the teachers RL-induced policy shifts. These students span three scales and dense and MoE architectures within one family with compatible tokenizers. The transfer objective does not require the teacher to outperform the student. We report all three teacher checkpoints and the Base students in the result tables to show pre-transfer performance. Training and evaluation data. Math transfer uses DAPO-Math-17K prompts (Yu et al., 2025). We evaluate on seven benchmarks: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT February 2025, HMMT November 2025, HMMT February 2026, and AMC 2023. For each problem, mean@32 measures average correctness over 32 generated responses. Benchmark scores average these values over problems, and Avg. is the unweighted mean across benchmarks. Code transfer uses Codeforces-derived prompt set. Evaluation uses the 378-problem MBPP+ set from EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023), reporting both the original MBPP tests (Austin et al., 2021) and the original plus additional tests (MBPP+), together with LiveCodeBench v4, v5, and v6 (Jain et al., 2025). We report mean@8, which averages correctness over eight generated responses per problem and then over the problems in each benchmark. Code Avg. is the unweighted mean over these five evaluation scores. Within each benchmark, methods share prompt templates, decoding parameters, maximum generation lengths, and sample counts. Student checkpoint selection. For both domains, we use AIME 2024 as the validation set and select each trained students checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy. All benchmark results for that student use this selected checkpoint.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Implementation. We build on verl (Sheng et al., 2025) and score the students top-16 token IDs with the three frozen teachers. The transfer objective combines the dense distillation reward with the student KL penalty. Answer graders are used only for evaluation. Implementation and training/evaluation configurations appear in Appendices and C.

sections.title: 4.2 BASELINES AND CONTROLS
sections.content: We compare against the Base student, standard on-policy distillation (OPD) from the Final teacher (Agarwal et al., 2024), OPD2 with its sampled-token objective (Heo et al., 2026), and endpoint Direct-OPD using log π1 log π0 (Feng et al., 2026). All methods share training and evaluation settings, except for method-specific hyperparameters. Three controls on Qwen3-8B math retain centering and alter one component of the full method. No gate sets gt = 1 while retaining the gate-mean normalization rule. Shuffled gate permutes gates among valid response prefixes within batch, retaining each prefixs candidate weights and centered endpoint signal. No normalization fixes κB = 1 while retaining the positive-cosine gate. Appendix gives definitions and invariants of the shuffle control. We separately vary the math Waypoint over teacher RL steps 500, 600, and 700 on Qwen3-8B in Appendix F.

sections.title: 5 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: We compare transfer performance across math and code at three student scales (Section 5.1). We examine learning trajectories and performance relative to the Final teacher on Qwen3-8B math (Section 5.2). We assess the roles of temporal gating, gate assignment, and mean normalization through ablations (Section 5.3). 5.1 MAIN RESULTS ACROSS DOMAINS AND SCALES Tables 1 and 2 report math scores and code averages. Full code results appear in Appendix D. Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the evaluated student methods in all six settings. Math. Waypoint-OPD improves over Direct-OPD, the strongest average baseline for all three students, by 2.18, 1.59, and 1.89 percentage points for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30BA3B, respectively. It improves 19 of 21 benchmark comparisons. The exceptions are HMMT25N for 14B (47.60 to 47.08) and HMMT26F for 30B-A3B (33.05 to 32.77). These results demonstrate improvements over endpoint transfer across student scales and both dense and MoE architectures. The 14B and 30B-A3B students also exceed the Final teachers 56.13 average by 3.07 and 1.72 points, respectively, while 8B essentially matches it at 56.14. The 14B student surpasses the teacher on all seven math benchmarks. Code. Waypoint-OPD improves over Direct-OPD by 2.66, 1.52, and 1.19 percentage points on average for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, with gains in all 15 code comparisons. OPD2 achieves higher scores on 14B LCB v5 and on 30B-A3B MBPP and MBPP+, while Waypoint-OPD retains the highest average for each student (Appendix D). The 14B and 30BA3B students also surpass the Final teachers 55.37 average by 2.45 and 2.17 points, respectively, each scoring higher on four of the five code evaluations. Interpreting the endpoint comparison. The gains over Direct-OPD show that Waypoint-OPD improves transfer performance across both domains and all three student scales. OPD and OPD2 provide complementary comparisons with Final-teacher imitation and selective distillation based on advantage sign agreement, respectively. 5.2 LEARNING DYNAMICS Figure 3 compares Waypoint-OPD and Direct-OPD at matched evaluation steps during Qwen38B math training. Unlike the selected-checkpoint results in Table 1, these trajectories show the performance gap over the same 100 updates.

sections.content: Ablation insights. These ablations support temporal weighting, its prefix assignment, and an incremental benefit from normalization in Qwen3-8B math. Their gaps are conditional on the retained components, not independent additive contributions. For fixed rollout batch, shuffling preserves the gate distribution and κB, while advantage and gradient norms depend additionally on the gatesignal pairing (Appendix E). Supplementary diagnostics show stronger average gate attenuation in later batches, while mean-gate normalization does not fix the reward norm (Appendix G).

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: On-policy distillation and policy-shift transfer. Knowledge distillation transfers teacher distributions or generated sequences (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim & Rush, 2016), while on-policy variants supervise student-generated trajectories (Agarwal et al., 2024). Complementary work refines divergence objectives and the use of teacherand student-generated data (Wen et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024; 2025). Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether weaker supervision can elicit stronger capabilities (Burns et al., 2024). WSPO and proxy-tuning reuse weak models adaptation contrast for training and decoding, respectively (Zhu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024). Within on-policy training, Direct-OPD transfers an RL-induced policy change through an endpoint log-ratio on student rollouts (Feng et al., 2026). W2S-OPD constructs proxy teacher by adding weak-model logit contrast to student base logits, then minimizes reverse KL on student rollouts. Its contrasts span RL checkpoints, model scales, and correct versus incorrect hints (Yu et al., 2026). OPRD uses centered teacherreference shift to amplify the component of verifier-driven gradient along that direction (Park et al., 2026). Waypoint-OPD builds on Direct-OPD, weighting local endpoint signals by agreement between shifts before and after Waypoint checkpoint. Selective supervision in distillation. Teacherstudent compatibility affects the utility of on-policy supervision (Li et al., 2026). Prune-OPD uses support overlap for suffix attenuation (Yang et al., 2026). EOPD uses teacher uncertainty in its entropy-dependent forward KL (Jin et al., 2026), while PW-OPSD uses token position in its reference-conditioned self-distillation (Liu et al., 2026). OPD2 gates sampled-token updates by sign agreement between centered teacherbase and teacherstudent advantages (Heo et al., 2026), whereas RG-OPD gates trajectories using agreement between verifierderived advantages and teacherstudent sequence log-likelihood gaps (Akhondzadeh et al., 2026). Waypoint-OPD uses different evidence: consecutive shifts in the teachers own RL trajectory over student-supported candidate actions. Their weighted directional agreement produces prefix-level gate for the dense endpoint update, without verifier feedback during transfer. This agreement is weighting criterion, not guarantee of correctness. Checkpoint selection and progressive distillation. teachers final performance need not determine its teaching utility: early stopping and intermediate checkpoint selection can improve distillation (Cho & Hariharan, 2019; Wang et al., 2022). Pro-KD and progressive distillation use successive teacher checkpoints as targets or curriculum (Rezagholizadeh et al., 2022; Panigrahi et al., 2025). Direct-OPD also studies RL checkpoint choice for transfer (Feng et al., 2026). For fixed Initial and Final endpoints, Waypoint measures directional consistency between the two shifts. It supplies neither an imitation target nor curriculum. The centered Initial-to-Final shift remains the transferred object.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to transfer RL-induced policy changes. An intermediate Waypoint checkpoint reveals whether early and late changes in relative action preferences reinforce or oppose each other at student-generated prefixes. This information, unavailable from endpoint differences alone, determines the weight of the centered Initial-to-Final shift in the students on-policy objective. The method requires one additional frozenteacher scoring pass and no verifier calls during transfer. Experiments on mathematical and code reasoning show gains over endpoint transfer across three Qwen3 student scales. Ablations on Qwen38B math support prefix-specific gate assignment and batch-scale normalization. These findings suggest that intermediate teacher checkpoints provide evidence for weighting local policy changes during student learning.
